issue: A supervisor could hold four GPU locks while completed or not-yet-started lanes were idle.
root_cause: The generic ImageNet acceptance launcher acquired all four locks before validation and retained them for the full six-task supervisor lifetime.
The legacy DARTS DDP launcher used the same process-wide lock scope.
Python lock files retained an owner PID after normal unlock, which could be mistaken for an active lock.
Shell pipelines and forked Python workers inherited the lock descriptor, so an orphan descendant could retain the kernel lock after its supervisor exited.
remediation: Sequential DDP acquires the four-lock set for one active task and releases it before the next task.
Parallel single-GPU execution acquires and releases one lock per scientific task; packed execution holds one lock only while its concurrently packed tasks remain active.
Python gpu_lock clears owner metadata before unlocking.
The shell lock-holder closes its descriptor in the task subshell before launching Python or tee, and Python closes active lock descriptors in fork children.
Recovery checks kernel flock state and never deletes an active lock pathname.
validation: full pytest suite passed after the inheritance fix
limitations: The lock protocol coordinates only same-user zcp-test processes.
A lock file may exist while unlocked; only a non-blocking flock probe determines ownership.
Processes that bypass the protocol can still use the same physical GPU.

The already-running AutoFormer cohort started before this patch and was not restarted; both held locks currently correspond to active GPU work and the systemd control group contains its descendants. New launches use the corrected inheritance behavior.
